title: Wall Street Chiefs Split Over AI Boom as Financing Needs Reach Trillions
excerpt: At a Hong Kong summit, Blackstone and the big banks backed the AI buildout while Pimco, Bain Capital and Franklin Templeton warned that spending and valuations are outrunning returns.
body:
• At the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit on Tuesday, bank chiefs backed continued AI financing while big money managers warned spending and valuations are running ahead of returns, Bloomberg reported.
  • Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman said AI financing could reach about $10 trillion over five years and that about $550 billion in AI debt has been issued this year, according to CNBC's report of the summit.
  • Blackstone President Jon Gray said demand for computing power is running well ahead of supply, but the buildout will need more equity because lenders' exposure is concentrating.
  • JPMorgan Vice Chairman Daniel Pinto warned the market is pricing AI revenue growth too steeply and that a correction in the sector is possible.

The people financing the artificial intelligence boom used the same stage in Hong Kong on Tuesday to argue opposite conclusions from the same numbers. Bank chiefs said capital markets will keep funding the buildout; several of the world's largest money managers warned that the spending, and the debt behind it, is growing faster than the returns it must eventually produce. The remarks came at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit hosted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which drew about 280 senior finance figures, Bloomberg reported.

The Caution Camp: Too Much, Too Fast

Emmanuel Roman, chief executive of bond investor Pimco, warned that the scale of AI financing may prove to be "too much" for markets to absorb. Roman said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford's estimate, and noted that about $550 billion in AI debt has been issued in various forms so far this year, according to CNBC's report of the panel. Even with a mix of equity and debt, he said, the amount required is "gigantic" next to a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion. Bain Capital Chairman John Connaughton said some AI assets are already valued very highly, and the key question is whether investors can earn returns to match. Franklin Templeton CEO Jenny Johnson said the biggest cloud companies are turning from businesses that need little capital into ones that need a lot, and that the AI investment cycle may have become overextended.

The Bankers: Demand Is Real, Financing Will Come

Blackstone President Jon Gray, whose firm is an active investor in AI infrastructure, said companies will need to raise more capital to meet demand — and that the demand justifies it. "Now you're in an environment where the demand's running well ahead of supply," Gray said, citing "pretty extraordinary" demand for computing power, according to Reuters. Gray added that "some of this scepticism today is probably healthy," but argued the buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become increasingly exposed to the companies driving it — a concentration risk for debt investors across the sector and at individual firms. Blackstone agreed last week to provide $63 billion in financing with Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, Reuters reported.

"Now you're in an environment where the demand's running well ahead of supply."

— Jon Gray, President, Blackstone

Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon said strong companies with "good stories" would still be able to raise capital despite AI-related market upheavals, while conceding the industry's growth could create volatility. "Investors will find situations where they pick wrong, where they lose money," he said. "It's important to have a balanced, diversified view." Goldman wrote in a report on Monday that global data center demand would require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years. Morgan Stanley Chief Executive Ted Pick put the buildout's cost at $10 trillion to $15 trillion over the next decade, said it could add 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points to real GDP growth, and warned that some projects with weak finances will not last, Bloomberg reported.

The Numbers Behind the Argument

The dispute is about arithmetic, not about whether AI works. Combined AI spending is set to exceed $730 billion this year, up from about $700 billion, according to Reuters, and S&P expects the top six US hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta and SpaceX — to spend more than $7 trillion on data centers and other AI-related capital expenditure between 2025 and 2030, while running negative free cash flow until at least next year. The latest test of investor appetite came on Monday, when Google parent Alphabet sold €6 billion ($6.7 billion) in bonds. Asia-Pacific tech fundraising, meanwhile, more than tripled to $125.8 billion in the first three quarters of 2026 from $36 billion a year earlier, LSEG data shows.

JPMorgan Vice Chairman Daniel Pinto landed between the camps: bullish on AI itself, but convinced the market is pricing in revenue and earnings growth that is too steep. "I do believe that it has a positive, slow curve and it may not be as steep as the market is pricing," he said. "So I think that it could be a correction in the AI sector." Citadel Securities CEO Peng Zhao said the sheer scale of capital and growth in AI is proving difficult for some investors to value correctly, adding to volatility. The summit followed a sharp fall in technology shares in October, after results including Alphabet's latest quarter raised fresh doubts about whether heavy AI spending will pay off — the question none of the speakers, on either side, claimed to have settled.
